audioScript:
Good morning, Midya. It's Friday, June twenty-sixth, twenty twenty-six. Here's what matters today — and there's quite a bit that matters.

Let's open with the story that should be front of mind for every Canadian university leader and every consultant who works in that space: Canada's international student crisis just got a headline number, and it's staggering. Prime Minister Mark Carney confirmed this week that international student arrivals have fallen sixty percent. Not five percent, not fifteen — sixty. Foreign worker numbers have halved in the same period. Carney framed this as Canada taking back control of immigration, which is a politically useful phrase, but the operational reality for every college and university in this country is a funding earthquake.

Here's the context worth holding. For roughly a decade, Canadian institutions — from UBC to Carleton to Thompson Rivers right here in Kamloops — built their financial models on international student tuition, which in many cases runs three to four times the domestic rate. That revenue cross-subsidized research, capital projects, and in some cases basic operations. A sixty-percent drop in arrivals doesn't just mean empty seats. It means deferred infrastructure, hiring freezes, program cuts, and in some institutions, genuine questions about financial viability.

And the source-country story makes it worse. India was Canada's single largest pipeline of international students for years. A separate story today from Firstpost documents how Canada has lost its appeal specifically among Indian students, who are now choosing Australia, the United Kingdom, Germany, and even the United States despite U.S. policy volatility. These students haven't stopped wanting to study abroad — they've stopped choosing Canada. That is a brand problem as much as a policy problem.

Why does this matter for your consulting practice? Because institutions that are losing enrolment revenue and facing an identity crisis as a study destination are exactly the clients who need strategic help — on brand positioning, on recruitment marketing, on how to tell a compelling story in competitive markets. They are not going to solve a sixty-percent decline by tweaking their website. They need a fundamentally different approach to how they present themselves globally, and they need someone who understands both marketing strategy and the international education landscape. That is your territory, Midya. The pain is real, the budgets are constrained but not zero, and the urgency is high. If you haven't already mapped the ten or fifteen Canadian institutions most exposed to this enrolment cliff, this weekend is a good time to do it.

There's also an interesting governance dimension to watch. The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives published a piece today arguing that so-called institutional neutrality at Canadian universities is a fiction — that claiming neutrality is itself a political act. This is a live debate on campuses right now, and it creates communications complexity for administrators who need to speak to international student markets, domestic donors, government funders, and faculty simultaneously. Institutions navigating that tension will need sophisticated strategic advice, not just PR.

Now to AI, where three stories today combine into one coherent picture of where the industry is heading.

First, the price shock. Apple raised MacBook and iPad prices by as much as twenty-five percent this week, explicitly blaming soaring memory chip costs driven by AI demand. Microsoft is in the same position. For years, the AI story was told in terms of its impact on jobs. Now it's showing up on device price tags, on subscription costs, and increasingly on the cost of every digital product and service built on top of AI infrastructure. For you as a marketing consultant who positions AI as a capability driver for clients, this is the moment to have a frank conversation about total cost of ownership. AI-powered marketing stacks are getting more expensive at the infrastructure layer, and clients need to understand that before they sign off on transformation roadmaps.

Second, and arguably the more strategically important AI story today: China's models are quietly winning the global adoption race. Not because DeepSeek or Alibaba's Qwen have beaten GPT-4o or Claude — they arguably haven't on pure benchmark performance. But they're available, they're cheap, and in many markets they're becoming the default. Axios reports today that U.S. export control strategy is described by experts as erratic — making decisions about model access on the fly — while China is systematically promoting open-source AI models through diplomatic and economic channels. For Canadian companies and institutions deciding what AI infrastructure to build on, this creates a genuine strategic question: do you bet on American platforms with uncertain access policies, or do you keep your options open? This is not a technical question. It's a vendor risk question, and it's one your consulting practice can help clients think through.

Third, the most tactically immediate AI story for marketers: at Cannes Lions this week, Amazon unveiled Alexa+ Agentic Ads, being tested right now with Papa Johns. The premise is that AI agents — not humans — will initiate purchases on behalf of consumers. An Alexa agent that knows you order pizza on Friday nights might surface a Papa Johns offer before you've consciously decided to order. The advertising transaction happens at the agent layer, not the human layer. This is agentic advertising, and it is no longer theoretical. If your clients are in retail, foodservice, or any category where repeat purchasing is the model, they need to understand that the next frontier of conversion optimization is influencing AI agents, not humans. The creative brief changes. The targeting logic changes. The measurement changes. Everything downstream of the consumer decision changes when the decision is being made by software.

Staying in marketing territory, there are two pieces today worth your attention as you shape your consulting positioning.

The first is a SmartBrief piece on higher-ed visibility in the zero-click era. It addresses exactly the problem that every Canadian university's marketing team is staring at: AI-generated answers in Google and other search interfaces are eating organic traffic. When a prospective student asks an AI assistant "what's the best university in BC for international students," they get a synthesized answer — not a list of blue links they click through. If a university's brand and content aren't being ingested and represented accurately by those AI systems, they're invisible at the most critical moment in the recruitment funnel. This is a legitimately new problem that most in-house marketing teams don't have the skills or frameworks to address. It's also a natural entry point for a consultant who understands both AI and brand strategy.

The second is an Adweek piece from yesterday, produced in partnership with Adobe, about whether brands can engineer cultural moments rather than simply react to them. The tension at the centre of the piece is one you'll recognise from your own practice: cultural relevance is by definition spontaneous and authentic, but brand campaigns are by definition planned and produced. The answer the piece points toward is creating the conditions — the creative latitude, the rapid response infrastructure, the cultural listening systems — that allow a brand to act fast enough to feel native to a moment rather than opportunistic. For a marketing consultant working with institutional clients who tend to be slow and consensus-driven, this is a useful framework: you're not selling speed, you're selling readiness.

Locally, two Kamloops stories worth a moment.

The good news: the $386 million Kamloops Cancer Centre is on track for its 2028 opening, and active recruitment of medical staff is now underway. This is a significant milestone. When complete, it will meaningfully change the healthcare landscape for the entire interior of BC, including Sun Peaks. Residents who previously had to travel to Vancouver or Kelowna for cancer treatment will have access to a full-service facility in Kamloops. If you have family members in the region, this is the kind of infrastructure investment that makes staying in the interior a genuinely different proposition than it was five years ago.

The second local story is a useful communications case study. A post-incident review of the East Kamloops water outage found that the city's decision to use hyper-targeted emergency messaging — sending alerts only to the specific addresses affected — actually caused confusion. Residents who received no alert assumed they were fine; neighbours who did receive one weren't sure if it applied to adjacent properties. The debrief concluded that precision targeting backfired because people's mental model of an emergency is neighbourhood-scale, not parcel-scale. There's a genuine marketing lesson here: segmentation and personalisation are powerful tools, but they can undermine the social proof and shared-experience dynamics that make communications feel credible. Something to keep in the back of your mind when advising clients on crisis communications or community engagement.

Two global stories to round out your situational awareness.

Ukraine launched one of the largest drone strikes of the entire war overnight — 660 drones targeting twelve Russian regions and Crimea simultaneously. Russian air defences intercepted them, but the scale signals a meaningful shift in Ukraine's offensive posture. This is not a battlefield development that directly affects your day, but it is relevant context for any client work touching European markets, supply chains with Eastern European exposure, or energy markets, which remain volatile.

On the economic front, new U.S. data out Thursday shows that Americans are still spending robustly despite rising energy costs and persistent inflation. Income growth is accelerating faster than demand is being suppressed by high interest rates — which is complicating the new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's job considerably. The short version: the U.S. consumer is not cracking, which is good for North American business confidence but raises real questions about whether rates will fall as fast as markets have been pricing. For Canadian businesses watching cross-border demand and for anyone with variable-rate exposure, this is worth tracking.

One longevity note today, and it's genuinely interesting rather than alarming.

STAT News published a clear explainer this morning on pulmonary hypertension — a serious and often underdiagnosed condition where high pressure in the lungs strains the right side of the heart — and why a new GLP-1 drug application is generating interest in that space. GLP-1s, the class of drugs that includes Ozempic and Wegovy, have already demonstrated cardiovascular benefits well beyond weight loss. The emerging hypothesis is that their anti-inflammatory and metabolic effects may also help in pulmonary hypertension, which currently has limited treatment options. This is early-stage, but it's another data point in the broader story of GLP-1s as systemic metabolic modulators rather than just appetite suppressants. If you're tracking the longevity and preventive health space as it intersects with your own health planning or your family's, the GLP-1 story continues to expand in meaningful ways.

That's your Friday briefing, Midya. The dominant thread today is Canadian higher education in genuine crisis — and genuine crisis creates genuine consulting opportunity if you move thoughtfully. The sixty-percent enrolment drop is your opening, the zero-click visibility problem is your service line, and the institutions most exposed are your prospect list. Spend some time this weekend thinking about how you want to position your practice specifically for that moment. You're well ahead of most of the market in having both the AI fluency and the institutional understanding to help. Use it. Have a strong Friday.
